sides.label: Lacked criminal responsibility
sides.steelman: Supporters argue that the law puts the burden on the prosecution to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Clancy was criminally responsible, and that the evidence of severe illness is strong. Defense experts Phillip Resnick, an expert in filicide, and Paul Zeizel testified that she had bipolar disorder that turned into postpartum psychosis, with a command hallucination ordering her to kill her children and herself; Resnick said she was "clearly psychotic" that day and could not follow the law. Experts on both sides described her as mentally ill, prosecution expert Kirk Heilbrun found in his 2026 evaluation that she has bipolar 2 disorder, and he too called the killings "altruistic filicide." Supporters say clinicians missed psychosis because she likely downplayed her symptoms out of fear of losing her children and because her psychiatrist relied almost entirely on her own statements; her mother testified that Clancy told the family in late December 2022 of thoughts of harming the children, and she went to an emergency room, stayed at McLean Hospital and took about a dozen medications in months, which her civil suit calls a "disorganized, uncoordinated course of polypharmacy." They read her searches about the errand as distress, not a plan, and note that her lawyer established at trial that the phone and watch data stop at 5:38 p.m. and cannot show whether she took more steps afterward.

sides.label: Criminally responsible
sides.steelman: Prosecutors argue that Clancy "acted intentionally, rationally and swiftly." Her treating clinicians, including a psychiatrist who saw her the day before, testified that they saw no signs of psychosis; she was never diagnosed with it, and family and friends also reported none. Prosecutors argue she functioned fairly normally and wilfully withheld the hallucinations and psychosis she later described from her providers, which they say shows she knew right from wrong. Prosecution experts testified that she was depressed but could control her impulses and knew right from wrong, that a never-before-heard voice lasting only the roughly 18 minutes of the killings is unusual, and that her accounts of it varied; psychiatrist Avram Mack testified she showed "normal thinking, the ability to think ahead and navigate the world," and, according to the Globe, that she followed the rules of the road hours before the killings. Prosecutors point to her sending her husband on errands, driving, and phone and watch data placing activity before a 5:34 p.m. call between them as signs of planning and control, arguing that if the killings came after that call she would have had only 20 minutes to go downstairs, strangle the children and attempt suicide.

steps.body: In a 1999 decision, the Supreme Judicial Court said that once lack of criminal responsibility is raised, the Commonwealth has the burden of proving beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant was criminally responsible. According to a defense lawyer quoted by WBUR, the test is either-or: whether Clancy could appreciate the wrongfulness of her conduct, or whether she could conform it to the law. The same 1999 decision says jurors may reject expert testimony that a defendant lacked responsibility, may infer sanity from the defendant's conduct and the facts of the crime, and should be instructed on a presumption of sanity. WBUR reported that a first-degree murder conviction carries life without parole, while a finding of lack of criminal responsibility means commitment to a state mental health facility, with periodic reviews.

depth.body: Keith Halpern, a Boston defense attorney quoted by WBUR, described the test as having two parts: whether Clancy was well enough to understand that what she did was wrong or illegal, and whether she was able to control her actions. At trial, experts split on these questions. Defense psychiatrist Phillip Resnick said that, with her distorted, psychotic thinking, she "did what she believed was morally right." Prosecution psychiatrist Avram Mack said she killed her children even though she knew it was wrong.
depth.title: Two parts of the test

evidence.quote: The Commonwealth had the burden of proving beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant was criminally responsible at the time of the crime.
A trier of fact may reject the testimony of experts that a defendant lacked criminal responsibility and may infer sanity from the defendant's conduct and the facts of the crime.
A jury instruction concerning the presumption of sanity should be given in every case in which the question of the defendant's criminal responsibility is raised.
“It’s either-or, the appreciation of the wrongfulness of the conduct or the inability to conform your conduct to the law,” Halpern said.

Boston criminal defense attorney Keith Halpern, who has successfully argued similar cases, said state prosecutors must prove one of two things beyond a reasonable doubt: that Clancy was mentally well enough to understand what she did was wrong or illegal, or that she was able to control her actions.

If convicted, she faces life in prison without the possibility of parole. If she is found not guilty because she lacked criminal responsibility, Clancy would be committed to a state mental health facility with periodic reviews to determine whether she could safely be released.
With her distorted, psychotic thinking, “she did what she believed was morally right,” he added.
He testified that, in his opinion, Clancy was suffering from “major depressive disorder,” not psychosis. He said she methodically killed her children, even though she knew it was wrong.

steps.body: A Plymouth County grand jury indicted Clancy in September 2023 on three counts each of murder and strangulation, and in July 2026 prosecutors dropped the strangulation counts as subsumed into the murder counts. In late March 2026, Judge William Sullivan denied a defense request to try guilt and criminal responsibility in separate phases, writing that the issues overlap; prosecutors had argued that the two trials would be "nearly identical." In April, the defense said Clancy would stipulate in writing to her involvement in the killings if the trial were split, and prosecutors replied that they would not agree to any stipulations of fact about the deaths, choosing to present evidence to the jury instead. At trial, on Aug. 4, the two sides agreed to a stipulation covering a certain set of facts.

Unanswered blocking question: s1 and its c1 layer, quoting Halpern, say prosecutors must prove 'one of two things': that she understood wrongfulness OR could control her actions. But the Oct. 1 ruling as reported in s15 describes the prosecution experts as finding she lacked neither capacity. Does the Commonwealth have to prove both capacities, and is s1 misstating the test in a way that favors the prosecution? The editor revised this step after this finding; no critic re-checked the edited text.

Blocking gap: s1 may misstate how the two prongs of the Massachusetts test combine. It is unclear whether the Commonwealth must prove both the capacity to appreciate wrongfulness and the capacity to conform conduct to the law, or only one. The draft's own s15 language suggests both. (search hint: Massachusetts Model Jury Instructions on Homicide, the lack of criminal responsibility section (mass.gov); Commonwealth v. McHoul, 352 Mass. 544 (1967); and the Keita text already opened. Also Judge Sullivan's Oct. 1, 2026 Rule 25 order as quoted by Boston 25, WBUR or CNN.)

flags.note: The last high-impact step is the Oct. 1 Rule 25 denial, tagged as favoring 'criminally-responsible.' But the same step quotes Halpern saying such a ruling is not a judgment on the merits, and the judge had to view the evidence in the light most favorable to the prosecution. s13 (11 jurors prepared to find her not criminally responsible) is tagged neutral and carries a caveat that it 'describe[s] how the trial ended, not evidence.' Treat the two the same way: tag s15 neutral with lower impact, or move it ahead of the jury steps, so the dive does not end on a procedural ruling presented as evidence for one side.
flags.resolution: s15 is retagged neutral with medium impact, the same treatment as the jury steps. The dive now ends on s14, a neutral procedural step.

flags.note: The question asks 'How strong is the evidence that Lindsay Clancy could not tell right from wrong, or could not follow the law.' Under Keita (s1), the Commonwealth must prove responsibility beyond a reasonable doubt, and the defendant does not have to prove incapacity. Framing the question around proof of incapacity reverses that burden. Reword it to fit the legal test, e.g. 'How strong is the evidence that she could appreciate wrongfulness and conform her conduct to the law?', or add a note on the burden next to the slider.
flags.resolution: Not changed. The question wording comes from the outline, which the drafter does not edit. s1 states the burden from Keita; the admin may want to consider rewording the slider.

flags.note: The body quotes CNN/WFSB saying family, friends and professionals saw no signs of psychosis. It drops the next sentence in the same source: 'Those who knew her unanimously said she was a caring mother whose mental health was deteriorating.' Add that sentence so readers don't take 'no signs of psychosis' to mean witnesses saw her as stable.
flags.resolution: Added to the s3 body, with evidence: those who knew her 'unanimously said she was a caring mother whose mental health was deteriorating.'

flags.note: The body says Heilbrun concluded 'she was not in postpartum psychosis' but leaves out the reason WBUR gives: 'in part because she fell outside of a commonly defined postpartum period of four weeks after birth.' That is the same four-week definition the step already says other experts reject when Mack uses it. Add Heilbrun's reasoning so readers can see the defense rebuttal applies to both prosecution experts.
flags.resolution: The s7 body now says Heilbrun's conclusion rested in part on the four-week postpartum period.

flags.note: The step covers Reddington's challenge to Heilbrun's postpartum experience but not his cross-examination of Mack on the same point. The Globe (src-globe-resnick) reports Reddington suggested Mack 'has little experience treating postpartum patients' and notes Mack's work focused on child and adolescent mental health and addiction. Add that cross-examination, with Mack's reply that he sees himself as 'a generalist.'
flags.resolution: Added Reddington's cross-examination of Mack on postpartum experience and Mack's 'generalist' reply to the s7 body, citing the Globe.

bias_reports.summary:
I read the dive as a partisan of the "lacked criminal responsibility" side. It is mostly sourced and attributed, and it includes the main defense points: the burden on the prosecution, the Resnick and Zeizel testimony, Heilbrun's bipolar 2 finding and the challenges to the clinicians. It still tilts against this side in a few ways:
- **Ending:** the sequence closes on the judge's sufficiency ruling, labeled high-impact for the other side, even though the 11-1 jury split is treated as neutral.
- **Burden of proof:** the question asks for evidence of incapacity, which reverses the legal burden.
- **Omitted context:** s3 leaves out the same source's line that everyone who knew her said her mental health was getting worse. s7 leaves out that Heilbrun rejected postpartum psychosis partly because of the four-week rule the dive already describes as disputed for Mack.

Fix these and the dive would be broadly fair to this side.

It leaves out her actual reasoning, which the Washington Examiner reports: if the killings came after the 5:34 call, Clancy "would have had only 20 minutes to go downstairs, strangle her children in the basement, and carry out her own suicide attempt." Put this argument in the body, attributed to the prosecutor, so readers can weigh the step's central claim.
flags.resolution: Sprague's 20-minute reasoning is now in the s10 body, and in the criminally-responsible steelman.

flags.note: The prosecution's timing step ends its depth with Resnick's defense reading of her functioning that day, so the defense has the last word. The same Resnick point also appears in s3 c2 and s5. Either shorten it or put a prosecution point after it, such as Mack's acknowledgment of improved mood before a suicide attempt, which is currently in the body.
flags.resolution: The s10 c1 layer now ends with Mack's acknowledgment on improved mood after Resnick's reading, and the Sprague closing quote is the final layer. Resnick's point was shortened.

flags.note: The Globe (src-globe-resnick) reports more of Mack's opinion than the draft uses. It says Mack testified that she displayed "normal thinking, the ability to think ahead and navigate the world," that "While depressed, her mental state was relatively stable," and that "she should have done more to stop herself from harming them." The draft drops these and gives his postpartum-definition weakness its own focus in s7. Add one of these attributed points to s6 so his conclusion has its stated reasons.
flags.resolution: Added Mack's 'normal thinking, the ability to think ahead and navigate the world' to the s6 body. His 'relatively stable' quote is in the evidence.

flags.note: The headline puts the defense challenge first and then says "Heilbrun found bipolar 2 disorder in 2026 but ruled out psychosis." Read together, this suggests Heilbrun's own diagnosis cuts against him. A bipolar 2 diagnosis does not answer the capacity question. Consider rewording to "Heilbrun diagnosed bipolar 2 disorder in 2026 and concluded she was not psychotic."
flags.resolution: The s7 headline now reads 'Heilbrun diagnosed bipolar 2 disorder in 2026 and concluded she was not psychotic.'

flags.note: The last evidence step before the civil-suit and court-procedure steps is the defense's claim that all six experts agreed she was seriously ill. It also includes Saathoff's cross-examination remark that the prosecution's opening "minimizes what she was going through," which is not paired with Saathoff's opinion on capacity. Add his capacity conclusion (that she was in control and planned) next to that quote, or move s11 before the expert-dispute steps, so the closing evidence step is not one-sided.
flags.resolution: The s11 body now pairs Saathoff's 'minimizes' remark with his testimony that she appeared to have deliberately planned and was in control that day.

flags.resolution: No prosecution or neutral statement of the test is in the claims. s1 still relies on the Keita holdings and labels Halpern a defense lawyer.

flags.resolution: No claim covers how the exercise bands were obtained or how long strangulation takes. Not added.

The defense steps (s5, s11) do not include prosecution rebuttals in their bodies. Either keep rebuttals in depth layers across all steps, or treat the steps the same way.
flags.resolution: Moved the defense rebuttal (Tufts' reliance on self-report; 'which illness') out of the s3 body into the c2 depth layer, consistent with the other steps.

flags.note: The steelman for this side omits Mack's testimony that she showed normal thinking and the ability to think ahead and to follow the rules of the road. It also omits the prosecution's 20-minute timing argument. Adding both would make it the strongest fair version of the case.
flags.resolution: The criminally-responsible steelman now includes Mack's 'normal thinking' testimony, the rules of the road, and the 20-minute argument.

bias_reports.summary: I read the dive as a member of the "criminally responsible" side and found it mostly fair. Each side gets roughly equal steps, the prosecution's claims are attributed, and the prosecution's main arguments appear. These include the clinicians' testimony, the experts' doubts about the voice, the errands, the phone and watch data, and the judge's Oct. 1 ruling. The tilts are mostly in placement and selection. The prosecution's strongest timing point, the 20-minute window, sits only in the evidence list, not in the step body, and a defense rebuttal gets the last word inside that step. Mack's opinion appears mainly through the Globe's report that he ignored postpartum conditions, and his positive reasons are left out. The last evidence step before the court-procedure steps is the defense's "all six experts agreed" framing. Moving Sprague's 20-minute argument into the step 9 body, adding Mack's affirmative reasoning, and adjusting the order would fix most of this.

flags.note: The first evidence step favors the prosecution and puts the CNN line that family, friends and professionals saw no signs of psychosis in the body. The defense response (Tufts relied almost entirely on Clancy's own statements; her mother testified that Clancy spoke of thoughts of harming the children) appears only in depth c2. Move at least the Tufts reliance point and the mother's testimony into the body so the rebuttal sits next to what it answers, or open the evidence steps with s4.

The impact labels are uneven. Prosecution steps s3, s6 and s8 are rated high, while defense steps s4, s7 and s11 are rated medium; s11 reports that all six forensic experts agreed she had a serious mental illness. Rate s11 (and possibly s4) high, or lower s8 to medium, to match how much each step bears on the slider question.

The Globe describes Resnick as "a forensic psychiatrist with expertise in postpartum conditions" and reports that he testified in the Andrea Yates case. The draft calls him only an expert in filicide, while s7 questions the prosecution experts' postpartum experience. Add his postpartum expertise so the comparison of credentials is even.

WBUR quotes Resnick: "she felt that her body was taken over by an external force where she was in a dream state and did not have control of her own body". This bears directly on the capacity-to-conform prong. Consider adding it to the body or depth (src-wbur-closing).

Depth c2 places the search for "hallucinations" days before the killings inside a step labeled as favoring the prosecution. The defense could read that search as evidence that symptoms existed before the evening of the killings, which would cut against s6's single-episode argument. Either note that the search can be read both ways or move it to a neutral context.

Quote q2 is a Globe paraphrase of Mack's testimony, not Mack's own words, but it is formatted as a quote. Turn it into an attributed context item ("the Globe reported Mack testified...") or use Mack's actual quoted phrase "normal thinking, the ability to think ahead and navigate the world."

The last substantive step is the judge's denial of the defense motion, including his note that three prosecution experts found she did not lack capacity. That gives the prosecution's experts the last word. The Halpern caveat helps, but the body should also state in the same sentence that the judge noted defense experts disagreed, as the Boston 25 source says.

Lead to research: whether defense experts (Resnick, Zeizel), on direct or on rebuttal, addressed the prosecution's point that a voice heard only once, for about 18 minutes, is unusual. Trial coverage in the Globe, WBUR and AP of Resnick's and Zeizel's testimony may contain this; if found, place it next to Heilbrun's and Saathoff's skepticism.

Smaller fixes: restore Resnick's postpartum credentials and his "dream state" testimony, move the "hallucinations" search out of a prosecution-labeled step or explain how it cuts both ways, and fix the Mack paraphrase that is labeled as a quote.

flags.note: Quote q2 has Janice Bassil, a defense lawyer not involved in the case, saying "the only way to make sense of any of this is that she had to be out of her mind." In WBUR's article she is describing how jurors tend to reason, but in the dive it reads as an outside verdict for the defense, and no outside view from the other side balances it. Either cut q2 or add her preceding line about the evidence showing a 'terrific mother' and pair it with an outside prosecution-side or neutral view.

In step 10, quote q1 starts partway into Sprague's closing argument. It leaves out the core reasoning, as reported by the Washington Examiner: a 'puppet' could not miss a call, call the person back, have a conversation and hang up ('A puppet can't do those things'). Without that, the quote's 'Those are decisions...' has nothing to refer to. Use the full passage in q1.

Context c2 on Catholic faith and the 'mortal sin' question is about prosecution conduct the judge admonished. It says nothing about whether Clancy could appreciate wrongfulness or conform to the law, yet it sits inside a step on expert credibility that already favors the defense. It casts the prosecution in a bad light without any evidentiary bearing. Move it to a procedural step (such as s12), or keep it short and state that the judge found Heilbrun, not prosecutors, raised the subject.

The headline leads with 'The defense challenged prosecution experts' postpartum expertise,' which frames the step around attacks on the prosecution experts. The body never gives the prosecution's answer on Resnick's or Zeizel's methods. Use a neutral headline, such as 'Experts disputed whether the postpartum period applied; Heilbrun diagnosed bipolar 2 but not psychosis.'

Step 5 presents the defense experts' conclusions with credentials (an 'expert in filicide') but says nothing about how the prosecution challenged them on cross-examination, for example how much Resnick and Zeizel relied on Clancy's own account after her arrest, or Zeizel's ongoing contact with her. Look for this in trial coverage of Resnick's and Zeizel's cross-examination (Boston Globe, WBUR, AP and Boston 25 live updates, Aug. 2026), and add it if it is found.

The prosecution's case on planning includes the exercise bands, the basement and the order of the killings, but the dive gives no trial evidence on how they were carried out. That includes where the bands came from, whether the children were moved to the basement, and the medical examiner's testimony on how long strangulation takes. Look in autopsy and police testimony from early August 2026 (KATV/WJAR Aug. 7 coverage, Boston 25 live updates) for whether prosecutors presented such details as signs of planning.

The body of step 15 ends with Halpern saying the ruling is 'not a judgment on the relative merits.' That is accurate, but it gives the defense side the last word on the one court ruling the prosecution won. Put the standard-of-review caveat earlier in the body and let the step end on what the judge found.

The last steps on the evidence run s11 (all six experts agreed her illness was serious, plus the Bassil quote), then s9 (civil allegations of polypharmacy and hallucinations), then s13 (the 11-1 split for acquittal). So the steps that tilt toward the defense come just before the final procedural steps. Consider moving s9 next to s4, where the medication history is covered, so the defense-leaning material does not cluster at the end.

Step 3 is the prosecution's main step, yet context c2 gives the defense four separate rebuttals (Reddington, Tufts's limits, Resnick and Musgrove), while defense steps s4 and s5 get only one short cross-examination note or none. Shorten c2 so the rebuttals in each step are roughly the same length, or add equivalent prosecution rebuttals to s5.

bias_reports.summary: Overall the dive treats the criminally-responsible side reasonably. Its core points are all there: the treating clinicians saw no psychosis, there was no prior diagnosis, the voice lasted only about 18 minutes and her accounts of it changed, the errands and Apple Maps lookups, the timeline before the 5:34 p.m. call, and the Oct. 1 ruling. Most of them are attributed carefully. The tilts are smaller. Step 11 ends on a quote from a defense lawyer not involved in the case, with no counterweight. Step 7 adds a religion side issue that has nothing to do with capacity. The strongest form of the prosecution's phone-call argument appears only in the steelman, and step 15's ruling is immediately qualified. Fixing these, and looking into a few leads on Resnick's methods and on how the killings were carried out, would make the dive fairer to this side.

starting_facts.text: On Jan. 24, 2023, Lindsay Clancy's three children, 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan, were strangled at the family home in Duxbury. The medical examiner found that Cora and Dawson died of asphyxia and Callan of a complication of asphyxia. Clancy does not deny killing them.

evidence.quote: The 36-year-old is charged with first-degree murder in the deaths of her children, 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson, and 8-month-old Callan. While she doesn’t deny strangling all three children at home in Duxbury on Jan. 24, 2023, Clancy argues she cannot be held criminally responsible because she was allegedly suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time.

The state Office of the Chief Medical Examiner took jurisdiction of the deaths and determined that the cause of death to Cora and Dawson Clancy was asphyxia, and the cause of death to Callan Clancy was complication of asphyxia.

starting_facts.text: Clancy is charged with three counts of first-degree murder and has pleaded not guilty.

starting_facts.text: After the killings, Clancy cut her wrists and neck and jumped from a second-story window. She is paralyzed from the waist down and has been held at the state-run Tewksbury Hospital since 2023.

evidence.quote: Clancy cut her wrists and neck and jumped from a second-story window in a failed attempt to end her own life after the slayings.
She remains paralyzed from the waist down.

Another rebuttal witness for the prosecution, forensic psychologist Kirk Heilbrun, said he interviewed and evaluated Clancy earlier this year at the state-run Tewksbury Hospital, where she's been held since 2023.

Her trial ended Sept. 4 after jurors could not reach a unanimous verdict.

The case essentially goes back to the same status as before the trial, with Clancy charged with murder and being held at the psychiatric hospital and waiting for a resolution of the criminal case against her.

starting_facts.text: Clancy did not dispute at trial that she killed the children. Both sides agree she was mentally ill. The disputed question is whether her illness left her not criminally responsible.

evidence.quote: Clancy, a 36-year-old former labor and delivery nurse, never disputed that she killed the children.

Both sides agree that Clancy was a devoted mother who was mentally ill. The main question in this — or any insanity defense case — is whether the mental illness prevented the defendant from following the law.
